title: A pricing page for a nonprofit
metaTitle: What a nonprofit pricing page should show
excerpt: State whether a program is free, fee-based, or gift-funded, and what each figure includes. Visitors use this page to judge fit before they give or join.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky, for a piece on seeing the shape of a cost from the ground.
caption: Buildings from the street, where the scale is obvious. A fee or a gift should be that legible. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What if the program is free to participants?
faqs.answer: Say so in the first screen. Free is a price shape. Then explain how the work is funded, and offer a way to give without implying that participants are being billed. Hiding 'free' so that everyone feels pushed to donate confuses both audiences.

faqs.question: How specific should suggested gift amounts be?
faqs.answer: Only as specific as the books. Tie an amount to a real expense your finance lead recognizes, or present the amounts as a ladder and link the report for program cost. A theatrical cost-per-outcome that you cannot defend will be the sentence a donor remembers.

faqs.question: Where do scholarships belong?
faqs.answer: On this page, with a shape. Who can ask, what you need from them, and when they hear back. Assistance available, with no path, sounds kind and behaves like a wall. If funds are limited, say they are limited.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A nonprofit pricing page is where a donor or a participant judges fit. They are not doing homework for its own sake. They want the shape of the cost: what is included, what is not, and how to give, join, or read the program. If they will ask the question anyway, the page should answer it.

The shape might be a program fee, a membership, a sliding scale, a free service with a published cost to deliver, or suggested gifts tied to real expenses. Pick the model you actually run. A page titled pricing that only says "every gift helps" has hidden the shape, and the visitor will assume you were unwilling to say.

## Name the model in the first screen

Say, in one or two sentences, how money works here. Participants pay a fee. Participants pay nothing, and gifts fund the program. Members pay dues and receive a defined set of things. Sponsors buy a defined package. Several of these can be true at once. They should not be blurred into a single warm paragraph.

Put the primary model first. If most people arrive to enroll, lead with the fee or with the fact that enrollment is free. If most people arrive to give, lead with what a gift funds, and still state the participant cost so nobody is misled. The order is an editorial decision about the audience you most need to serve this season. The facts of the other model stay on the page.

Label every figure. Per person, per month, per household, per event, per year. Say the currency. Say whether a fee is waived in a published circumstance. A number with no unit is how a family plans for the wrong amount and then feels tricked at intake. The trick may have been an accident. The trust cost is the same.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page helps someone do the thing they came to do. Here, that thing is a fit check. Can we afford to join, do we qualify for a waiver, does this gift pay for the program we think it pays for. A page that withholds those answers to seem flexible helps no one.

## What is included

For a participant fee, list what the fee covers. The weeks of the program, the materials, the meal, the supervision ratio if you publish it, the performance or the certificate if there is one. People compare this list to the number. A thin list under a large number needs a better explanation or a different number. A long list of vague benefits, community, growth, support, does not count as a list.

For a membership, list what a member can use. Hours, guest policy, voting rights, the newsletter if it is actually a benefit and not a burden. Note what requires an extra payment. Court time, a materials kit, a trip. The included set is the product. The extras are the boundary. Both belong in view.

For a gift, say what the fund pays for in categories a donor can check later. Staff hours for the clinic, food purchases, transit stipends, the share that keeps the lights on. You do not need a fake precision, "your fifty dollars buys this exact outcome," unless your books truly work that way and you can show the method. A honest category is better than a theatrical unit cost.

For a sponsorship or a ticket, say what the payer receives and what the organization receives. A table at a dinner is partly a purchase and partly a gift. Call both parts by their names. Surprising a sponsor with the tax language after they have paid is a messy conversation your page can prevent.

## What is not included

Exclusions are part of respect. The fee does not cover transportation. The program does not include childcare unless it does. The membership does not include private lessons. The gift does not direct staff to favor a named person. Write these as boundaries, in the same calm tone as the inclusions.

Scholarships and waivers need a shape too. Who can ask, what you need from them, and when they hear back. "Assistance available" with no path is a sentence that sounds kind and behaves like a wall. If funds are limited, say they are limited. If the answer is a payment plan with specific dates, say the dates. Participants plan their lives around these sentences.

Say what a donor cannot earmark, if that is your policy. Unrestricted gifts keep the program standing. Restricted gifts are possible above a threshold, or they are not. Publish the rule you will enforce. A donor who wants a building named will still ask. Everyone else will be relieved to see that ordinary gifts go to the work described on the homepage.

Refunds and transfers belong here when money changes hands. Event tickets, program deposits, memberships cancelled mid-year. The window, the amount, the method. A policy page can hold the long version. The pricing page should state the spine of it so people do not have to discover it in a crisis.

## Suggested gifts and the cost of the work

If you publish suggested amounts, tie them to a real expense you are willing to explain. A night of the clinic. A month of produce for the school program. The cost of one crew day. The link between amount and expense should be something your finance lead recognizes. If the amounts are simply a ladder, 25, 50, 100, 250, say they are a ladder and point to the report for the cost of the program. Do not dress a ladder up as a unit cost.

Offer a way to give a different amount. Suggested levels are a convenience. They are not a menu that exhausts generosity or need. And offer the non-cash path if you truly want it and can process it. Stock, a donor-advised fund, a workplace match. One sentence and a contact for the unusual cases. The common case should stay on the page and finish without a call.

Recurring gifts need the cadence and the cancellation path in the open. Monthly, until they stop, cancelled by a reply or a link you actually monitor. A recurring gift that is hard to stop will be remembered longer than the program. Make the stop as clear as the start.

If the program is free to every participant, say that in the first screen of this page, and then explain how it is funded. Free is a price shape. Hiding it, in the hope that everyone will donate, confuses participants and insults donors who wanted to know the service was free. You can ask for support in the next sentence. You should not bury the fact.

## How to give, join, or read from this page

The actions sit next to the model they belong to. A fee has an apply or register step. A gift has a give step. A reader who is not ready has a link to the program description and to the latest report. Three doors are fine when each door is specific. A single "support us" button that dumps every intent into one form is how applications and donations get lost in the same inbox.

Say what happens after each action. A receipt. A confirmation of the amount and the cadence. An intake reply within the window you keep. A seat held or not held. Match the words on the button to the words in the confirmation. If the button says "apply" and the next page says "donate," you have switched the person's intent without asking.

Keep the form or the checkout as short as the payment processor and the law allow. Name, contact, amount, the designation if you have more than one fund. Ask demographic questions later, or ask them as optional, with a reason. A long preamble of required profile fields before a person can finish a gift is a quiet tax on generosity.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) notes that an average page visit lasts a little less than a minute, and that readers get through only about a quarter of the words. The model, the included list, and the action have to live in the part people reach. A story about the founding gift, placed above the fee, will spend the minute before the shape appears.

## Make the page agree with intake

Read the page against what intake and the bookkeeper actually do. If the site says materials are included and intake asks families to buy a list, change one of them before you publish. If the site says gifts are unrestricted and the donation form forces a designation, change the form. The pricing page is a promise. The building has to keep it.

Date the fees. "Program year 2026" or "effective until the June board meeting" gives you a reason to edit and gives a visitor a reason to trust the number is current. Undated prices on a nonprofit site often mean the number survived from a previous director. Look at it on purpose.

Put the awkward cases in a short set of questions under the main shape. Reductions, corporate matching, whether a ticket is deductible, who to email for a pledge that does not fit the form. Answer them in two or three sentences. Link the long policy. The questions should be the ones your inbox already sees, not a borrowed list about philanthropy in the abstract.

## Publish a number you can say out loud

Have the person who answers the phone read the page aloud. If they flinch at a sentence, rewrite it until they would say it at a front desk. Then complete one test gift or one test registration, with a real card in a test mode or a small real amount you can refund. Confirm the receipt, the internal email, and the words the donor sees. A pricing page that the staff have only looked at is unverified.

The visual design should make the shape scannable. Model, included, excluded, action. Quiet type will do. A giant number with no unit, over a photograph of someone in distress, combines two failures. The number is unclear, and the picture is doing the work the program description should have done.

You can see how a public page keeps a specific offer in view by looking at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The standard to borrow is clarity. A visitor can tell what is being offered and what it costs them, in money or in attention, without a private explanation.

Once the shape is visible, the visitor looks for the work itself, named as programs rather than as a cloud of values. [The services page a nonprofit actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-nonprofit-actually-needs) is the next piece, because each program still needs an outcome, a boundary, and a way to give, join, or read.
